newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Afrikaners cautious in saving their tongue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Afrikaners cautious in saving their tongue.

text.p: Afrikaans speakers have launched a bid to prevent their language slipping into obscurity in the new South Africa, but the country's vexed history forces them to act with circumspection.

About 80 leading academics, writers, editors and business leaders met in the university town of Stellenbosch in late November to discuss the future of Afrikaans, condemned by many blacks as a language of oppression.

Since President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress won the country's first all-race elections in 1994, the profile of Afrikaans has dropped sharply in many spheres ranging from the state broadcaster to announcements on passenger aircraft.
In a sign of the sensitivities that make the issue a minefield, no politicians were invited to the Stellenbosch meeting.
Several speakers stressed the danger of participants appearing to be setting up an ethnic-based grouping trying to fight its corner against black majority rule.

"The question is: Will you unknowingly prepare for a demagogue or will you throw off the burden of history, albeit a burden of privilege?" Mahmood Mamdani, a visiting academic from Uganda, told delegates.
AFRIKAANS SEEN IN RETREAT
Jannie Gagiano, a University of Stellenbosch political scientist who attended, said the main concern was the marginalisation of Afrikaans.

"People were anxious about Afrikaans being 'privatised', being shifted out of the domain where it is part of the responsibility of the state to maintain it...especially as a medium of instruction in schools," he said. "In some areas Afrikaans is getting rolled back."

Gagiano said that in trying to free themselves of the past many Afrikaans-speakers now called themselves "Afrikaanses" rather than use the politically tainted "Afrikaner", the label which right-wing whites apply to themselves.

The rightwingers, heirs of those who imposed apartheid in 1948 and used their political power to promote Afrikaans, demand self-rule in a sovereign state as a way of avoiding what they call the yoke of black-communist dictatorship.
The right-wing Conservative Party expressed outrage at the way the Stellenbosch meeting handled the political dimension of promoting the language.
"For the Afrikaner, Afrikaans is a proud inheritance, a mother tongue received from God...A language which will be the first language of a free, sovereign republic," the party said.
It added that not everyone who spoke Afrikaans was necessarily an Afrikaner.

Afrikaans is one of the most widely used home languages in South Africa, with about six million people speaking it. But most mother-tongue Afrikaans speakers are mixed-race Coloureds, descended from liaisons between European settlers, Malaysian slaves and indigenous South Africans.

Those attending the Stellenbosch meeting included poet Breyten Breytenbach, who served a jail sentence in apartheid South Africa for helping the ANC, and Jakes Gerwel, a high-level Coloured official in Mandela's office.
Gagiano said the ANC government did not actively want to eradicate Afrikaans but did not have the resources to promote it as one of the 11 officially recognised languages.
He described apartheid history as a millstone around the neck of Afrikaans.
AFRIKANERS -- STRANGE BASTARDS?

"When Afrikaners organise, some people say 'Oh my God, these strange bastards, you can be sure they're marching somewhere'. But the environment has changed to such an extent that that sort of threat cannot be taken seriously any more," Gagiano said.
Bennie Bunsee, a member of the radical Pan Africanist Congress, represents those who are suspicious of attempts to organise behind Afrikaans.

"Instead of claiming a special language dispensation, Afrikaners need to realise that in Africa they must learn to love and speak African languages...They need to integrate with the African people," he said.
Afrikaans is spoken only in South Africa, although it has strong similarities with Dutch and Flemish and has borrowed some vocabulary and grammar from the Malay language.
The Afrikaans-language Die Burger newspaper said in an editorial that none of South Africa's language groups could claim to be without sin.
"And why does one minority language, English, get such a privileged position that in typical colonial style it achieves hegemony over the other 10 official languages?" the paper asked.
